subtopic: Building insurance and an emergency fund
subtype: Approach: comparing health policies on a checklist [Thinking]
passage:
Minakshi, put the kettle on and sit. You're about to choose a health policy, so let me tell you how I did it. I'm Trisha.
The agent who phoned me was smooth. "Just sign today, it's the best." I said no and took the brochures home.
I made a table. Down one side, several insurers; across, the things that matter: how much cover, how long before certain things are covered, the limit on room rent, what is left out, and how often the company actually settles claims. Then I read the small print, line by line, with a pencil.
Two policies that looked alike turned out very different on room rent and exclusions. That saved me from a nasty surprise.
The agent called back twice. I just said I'd decided.

qa.q: How many times did the agent call back?
What was Trisha probably feeling when the agent said "Just sign today"?
qa.a: Trisha was probably wary and unhurried, since Trisha said no and took the brochures home.

qa.q: Trisha chose to make a table and read the small print. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It showed how two similar-looking policies differed on room rent and exclusions, so Trisha avoided a nasty surprise.

qa.q: How might the agent have seen Trisha's refusal to sign on the spot?
qa.a: The agent probably saw a customer who would not be rushed, which is why the agent called back twice.

grounding: The elder's story shows a person comparing health policies on a checklist of cover, waiting periods, room rent limits, exclusions and claim record, and reading the small print.
